title: Communication, the Most Important Life Skill. Why Are Misunderstandings So Easy?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Cialdini, Robert B., Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion, New and Expanded, Harper Business 2021
Heath, Chip; Heath, Dan, Made to Stick: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die, Random House 2007

Civil Aviation Accident and Incident Investigation Commission (CIAIAC), Spain, final report on the collision of the KLM and Pan Am Boeing 747 aircraft at Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife, on March 27, 1977, Madrid 1978
Kruger, Justin; Epley, Nicholas; Parker, Jason; Ng, Zhi-Wen, Egocentrism over E-Mail: Can We Communicate as Well as We Think?, “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” 89 (2005)
Newton, Elizabeth L., The Rocky Road from Actions to Intentions, doctoral dissertation, Stanford University 1990

paragraphs: Elizabeth Newton, a psychology doctoral student at Stanford University, once asked participants in her study to tap out the rhythm of well-known songs with a finger, while others had to guess the titles. The tappers were convinced the listeners would get it right about every other time. Reality proved merciless: the listeners recognized just three songs out of a hundred and twenty. That was because the tapper heard the full melody in their head, instruments and all, while all that reached the listener was a dull, monotonous knocking on a tabletop. The same thing happens in everyday conversation: you know your intentions, but the other person gets only the words, and often understands something quite different from what you originally meant.

The First Book of Samuel shows perfectly what happens when words fail, and how much power they have when they hit the mark. For a long time David’s men had protected the flocks of wealthy Nabal out in the wilderness. When, at sheep-shearing time, David courteously asks for some hospitality, Nabal answers with an insult, and David immediately orders four hundred men to strap on their swords. Two short messages were enough to send several hundred men reaching for their weapons.

Nabal’s wife, Abigail, hears about everything. She reacts at once: she loads donkeys with bread, wine and meat, and rides out to meet David. She falls at his feet and begins with the words: “My lord, may the blame be on me alone” (1 Samuel 25:24). Although she was not the one who insulted him, she takes responsibility before she explains anything. Then she turns his attention to his future: when he becomes ruler of Israel, let him not be troubled by remorse for having shed blood needlessly and taken revenge himself (1 Samuel 25:31). She does not threaten him or lecture him; she reminds him of his long-term goals and of the responsibility that will rest on him as the future king. David gives up his revenge and blesses God, who sent her to meet him. Abigail tells her husband about everything only in the morning, once he has completely sobered up after the evening’s feast, because she knows that the right moment is a crucial part of every conversation.

Communication is a skill that can be learned. Assume that you may be misunderstood, and speak plainly about important matters. Begin with your own share of responsibility, and choose the time for a conversation with care. Abigail’s story shows that God often works through people who said a few clear sentences at the right time.

questions: Who do I owe one clear sentence?
challenge: Think of someone with whom you have an unresolved matter. Then put together one sentence that expresses your point of view simply.

paragraphs: On March 27, 1977, a tragic chain of events unfolded at the regional Los Rodeos airport on Tenerife. Two huge Boeing 747s were stuck in fog that was growing thicker by the minute. The Dutch KLM jet had already taken up its takeoff position and was about to start rolling. At that very moment the American Pan Am jet was taxiing in its path, barely visible because of the weather. The pilots of both giants were moving blindly, unable to see each other, and the staff in the control tower could do little to help them.

When the KLM first officer radioed that the crew was beginning the takeoff procedure, the controller replied with a laconic “OK” and then immediately told them to hold until they received official clearance. But in exactly the same split second, on the same frequency, the Americans began to speak. The two radio transmissions overlapped, producing a loud squeal in the headphones. As a result, the crucial part of the tower’s message, the part telling them to stay where they were, never reached the KLM cockpit.

The KLM flight engineer, however, had serious doubts. As the huge Boeing was already accelerating down the runway, he twice asked the pilots whether the Pan Am aircraft had definitely cleared the runway. The captain, a legend of the Dutch airline, its head of training and one of its most experienced pilots, replied with deep conviction that it had. The speeding aircraft could no longer be stopped. Some ten or fifteen seconds later came the collision, in which 583 people died. To this day it remains the deadliest accident in the history of world aviation.

Both aircraft were in perfect technical order. The disaster was decided by just a few sentences that people exchanged over the radio and inside the cockpit. How is it possible that professionals, for whom radio communication is the absolute foundation of their work, failed to understand one another? This tragedy invites an important reflection on our everyday conversations, which no one records, no one checks, and in which no one makes sure that the speaker’s intention has been correctly understood by the listener.

sections.heading: Tapping Instead of a Melody
paragraphs: The commissions investigating the accident later set out the whole chain of misunderstandings, link by link. The first officer’s report could be understood in two ways: as “we are ready for departure” or as “we are taking off right now.” The tower heard the first, though the crew meant the second. The controller replied with a word that was not one of the standard aviation phrases and could have sounded like permission. The flight engineer put his concern into a cautious question that was easy to brush off with a single word. And no one dared to contradict the captain any further, a man senior in rank and held in enormous esteem in the company.

The Tenerife tragedy forced aviation to change its language of communication completely. Today the word “takeoff” is heard on the radio only when the tower clears an aircraft for takeoff or cancels that clearance; in every other situation a different term is used. Much stricter attention is also paid to reading back every important instruction aloud, so that both sides can be sure the message has been correctly received. Communication training for crews was introduced as well, in which junior pilots learn to speak clearly about danger, even when that means challenging the captain. In a world where misunderstood information costs lives, pilots stopped taking things on trust and began rigorously verifying every message.

In everyday life, however, we work on exactly the opposite principle. In 1990 Elizabeth Newton, a psychology doctoral student at Stanford University, carried out an experiment in which she divided the participants into two groups. The first group’s task was to tap out on a tabletop the rhythm of well-known songs such as “Happy Birthday,” while the second group had to guess the titles from the tapping. Before the listeners had even said a word, the tappers estimated their chances of success: they were convinced it would work about half the time. The actual result was crushing: out of 120 tapped melodies, the listeners recognized just three.

Why such an enormous gap? The tapper heard the full melody in their head, words and all, while all that reached the listener was a dry knocking on the table. Exactly the same thing happens in everyday conversation. You know your intentions, the context behind them and everything you want to get across. The other person, meanwhile, hears only the words, and sometimes only some of them. This phenomenon has been called “the curse of knowledge”: once we know something, it is hard for us to imagine the perspective of someone who does not. We assume that because a matter is obvious to us, it must be just as clear to everyone else.

This is easiest to see in written messages. In 2005 a team led by psychologist Justin Kruger asked students to prepare short statements, either serious or sarcastic, and then pass them on to other people by email or by voice. The authors of both the emails and the recordings were optimistic: they expected the recipients to pick up their intention and tell a joke from a serious remark without difficulty 78 percent of the time. Those who listened to the voice recordings did in fact get it right 73 percent of the time. Those reading emails, however, managed only 56 percent, not much better than tossing a coin. Interestingly, the recipients of written messages were just as confident of their answers as those who heard a human voice. This happens because text loses tone of voice and facial expression, and the sender usually does not notice that key cues are missing from the message. So it is safer to deal with important and sensitive matters by phone, or better still, face to face.

sections.heading: Four Hundred Men with Swords
paragraphs: In the First Book of Samuel we read a story in which the lives of many people hang on just a few sentences. David is hiding from King Saul in the wilderness, with about six hundred armed men. Throughout the whole grazing season his men protect the flocks of wealthy Nabal of Carmel, and during that time the shepherds lose absolutely nothing (1 Samuel 25:7).

When sheep-shearing time comes, a season of celebration and generosity in that world, David sends ten men to Nabal with a courteous greeting and a request for some hospitality. Nabal, however, answers them with contempt. Who is this David anyway, he asks, and adds that there are plenty of servants these days running away from their masters (1 Samuel 25:10). The messengers return to David and give him a detailed report, and he issues a short order for every man to strap on his sword, then sets out for Carmel on a mission of revenge at the head of four hundred men. Two messages, a courteous request and an insult, were enough to send several hundred men reaching for their weapons.

Meanwhile, one of Nabal’s servants goes to his master’s wife, Abigail, and tells her what has happened. He speaks about his master without mincing words: Nabal is “such a scoundrel that nobody can speak to him!” (1 Samuel 25:17). Since there is no getting through to Nabal, his wife is the last resort.

This young servant does exactly what was missing in the cockpit on Tenerife. He goes to the person who can change the course of events and who stands much higher than he does in the household hierarchy. He presents the plain facts and adds his own testimony: David’s men were like a wall around the shepherds, by night and by day. He calls the danger by its name and ends with a clear request that his mistress think about what to do. He does not beat about the bush, but neither does he accuse anyone more than he has to.

Abigail acts immediately. She loads donkeys with two hundred loaves of bread, wine, the meat of five sheep, and cakes of raisins and figs, sends her servants ahead with the gifts and follows right behind them. She says nothing at all to her husband. She meets David on a mountain path at the very moment he is declaring that by morning not a single male of Nabal’s household will be left alive.

sections.heading: The Speech That Stopped Revenge
paragraphs: Abigail gets down from her donkey, falls at David’s feet and begins with a dramatic admission: “My lord, may the blame be on me alone” (1 Samuel 25:24). Although she was not the one who insulted him, she takes all the responsibility on herself in order to disarm the commander’s anger at once. Only after this gesture does she ask David to let her explain. Someone who hears such a deep apology finds it much harder to keep gripping the hilt of a sword, and much easier to really listen.

She says openly that her husband’s name means “fool” and that this is exactly what he is. She also explains that she did not see the messengers David sent. Then she does something quite unexpected: she stops going back over the past and begins to unfold a vision of the future of the man she is speaking to. She declares that the LORD will make him a lasting dynasty and that his life will be “bound securely by the LORD your God in the bundle of the living” (1 Samuel 25:29). The Hebrew speaks here of a small bundle, a pouch in which people carried their most precious things with them. So Abigail assures David that God holds his life close to Himself, like something very dear.

The most important sentence comes only at the end, when she turns to his future. When David has become ruler of Israel, let him not be troubled by remorse for having shed blood needlessly and taken revenge himself (1 Samuel 25:30-31). Abigail neither threatens nor lectures. She shows David his own future a few years from now and lets him decide for himself whether he wants to carry the weight of this one day for the rest of his life.

David answers with a blessing: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day! Blessed is your discernment, and blessed are you” (1 Samuel 25:32-33). He admits plainly that he has heeded her voice, and sends her home in peace. That day not one of the four hundred swords was used. A bloodthirsty army was stopped by one woman, a string of donkeys laden with bread and a few carefully chosen sentences.

There is also an ending that is easy to miss. Abigail returns home, where Nabal is holding a feast fit for a king and is thoroughly drunk, so she tells him nothing about what has happened until morning. She tells him everything only once he has sobered up (1 Samuel 25:36-37), because she knows that in the evening not one of her words would have got through to him.

sections.heading: A Skill That Can Be Learned
paragraphs: Both the tragic air disaster and the biblical story from Carmel teach the same lesson: good intentions are not enough. The captain, after all, wanted to take off safely, and David was convinced he had every right to retaliate. What decided everything was whether someone spoke the right sentence clearly, at the right moment and in a way the other side could accept. The flight engineer asked too cautiously, while Abigail spoke plainly, even though she was standing before an armed and angry man.

Effective communication is a set of skills that can be learned and practiced. Always assume that you may be misunderstood, and make a point of checking, rather than counting on the other person to read your mind. Speak plainly about important matters. Choose the right moment, and always begin with your own share of responsibility. Remind the other person of their long-term goals and their responsibility for the future, just as Abigail did with David.

It is hardest where hierarchy comes into play: in conversations with a boss, a parent or anyone who has the upper hand over you. The flight engineer was no exception. In aviation the phenomenon even has its own name. “Captainitis” is the syndrome of uncritical trust in a superior’s decisions, which leaves a leader’s obvious mistake uncorrected. That is why today’s training teaches a simple pattern: name your concern, state a hard fact and, finally, propose a concrete solution. In everyday life it sounds very similar: “I’m worried about this deadline. We have two days and we’re still missing data. I suggest we move the presentation back a week.”

This story also holds a deep truth about the way God works. Abigail stresses that it was the LORD who held David back from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:26), and David replies that it was He who sent her to meet him. Both of them understand perfectly well that the conversation on the mountain path became a place where God was at work. The Creator very often works in exactly this way: through a person who can say a few key sentences at the right moment. Your words, too, can become such a tool in someone’s life. It takes no great eloquence; sometimes all it takes is the courage to break the silence and be the first to start the conversation.

questions: Who do I owe one clear sentence?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Think of one person with whom you have an unresolved matter. Then put together one sentence that expresses your point of view simply.

**In action.** Go to that person, or arrange a short conversation with them. Bring something small: tea or something sweet. Begin with your own part, for example with the words: “In this matter I let you down in this and that respect.” Then say plainly, in one sentence, what you need. Finally, make sure the other person has understood what you wanted to tell them. If you cannot have this conversation today, plan when you will.
